posts:
Unusually destructive Pacific storms are battering California's coast in 2026. 🌐
Evidence: Warm waters, Tropical Storm Rachel, coastal flooding
#Climate #California #Aletheia

Forecasters report that anomalously warm Pacific waters are driving a historic hurricane season, sending tropical systems and heavy rain directly into Southern California.
Stated Judgement: (+0.15, +0.15) — Greater Good

While scientific data accurately records these rare storms, aging coastal infrastructure remains dangerously unprepared for recurring tropical flooding and high surf.
Resulting Judgement: (+0.00, +0.00) — Greater Evil

Verdict: CONDITIONAL — Fall into Destruction.
Integrity: Conditionally Sound (Hypocrisy: 1.5, z: 2)

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- The Conversation: PASS (+0.7, +0.6) — Accurate meteorological analysis.
- LA Times (Billy Crystal): COND (-0.4, -0.3) — Personal grief framing.
In 2026, El Niño and warm sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific have fueled rare tropical storms like Rachel, breaching historical weather norms in California.

The Bright Side:
Early storm warnings and modern forecasting gave vulnerable coastal communities critical time to prepare, preventing catastrophic loss of life.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The reporting occasionally confuses a localized meteorological anomaly with systemic collapse, substituting physical weather events for policy failures.

Social Physics Analysis:
Climate reporting navigates between objective scientific transparency and sensationalist dread. True resilience requires shifting from reactive disaster coping to proactive infrastructure reinforcement.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
When you map scientific transparency against infrastructural adaptation needs, it plots a direct trajectory toward Destruction. This reflects a shift toward empirical preparation.

The Unavoidable Truth: Warming Pacific waters are making rare California tropical storms an recurring reality.

The Unavoidable Lie: Coastal infrastructure is adequately prepared for extreme weather.

Alethekanon:
Data cannot be negotiated with. When physical thresholds shift, institutions either adapt their defenses or absorb the cost of willful blindness.

Awwthekanon:
It's heartbreaking to watch families lose homes to fires and storms in places that once felt safe. Nature asks for our utmost humility and care right now.

Brothekanon:
Wild year for weather. Hurricanes hitting Cali now? Crazy times, but at least the forecasts are giving people a heads-up before things flood out.

Spirithekanon:
"The people have forgotten God, and built strongholds; yet fire shall devour their palaces." Amos 2:5 PASS
Ignoring ecological realities while clinging to fragile structures invites inevitable reckoning.

Stated Claim / Post Context:
California is taking a beating from an unusually destructive 2026 Pacific hurricane season

=== MULTI-SOURCE TOPIC CLUSTER: California is taking a beating from an unusually destructive 2026 Pacific hurricane season ===

[Source 1 — theconversation.com] (URL: https://theconversation.com/california-is-taking-a-beating-from-an-unusually-destructive-2026-hurricane-season-294207):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
California is taking a beating from an unusually destructive 2026 Pacific hurricane season

Tropical storms rarely survive in the cool water off California, but waves from storms far to the south can still damaged coastal areas. And flooding rain can sweep in.

Actual Article Body:
Share article

Print article

California isn’t a place most Americans associate with tropical weather, but it’s taking a beating in 2026 from one of the most active eastern Pacific hurricane seasons in modern history.

For the second time ever, national forecasters issued a tropical storm watch for Southern California as Tropical Storm Rachel headed toward the region, bringing high tides, coastal flooding and drenching rain from Oct. 9-11. The first tropical storm watch was issued just three years earlier, for Hurricane Hilary.

The U.S. occasionally sees heavy rain from the remnants of Pacific storms that pass over Mexico and travel into the U.S. Southwest. But the 2026 season has been different. Three hurricanes deluged Hawaii as they passed close to the islands, a rare event for that state. And in September, Hurricane Marie churned up big waves that damaged oceanfront homes near Los Angeles before veering away from the coast.

Rachel weakened to an extratropical cyclone before its landfall in Baja California, but it brought high waves to Southern California that damaged more coastal homes and flooded streets. Its rainfall drenched communities from San Diego to the desert Southwest and even triggered flooding in Las Vegas.

I study Pacific hurricanes. While tropical storm impacts to California are unusual, they aren’t unprecedented. El Niño raises the risks.

Historically, Southern California has seen a few direct hits from tropical storms and numerous cases of damage from systems that remained offshore.

To find the earliest known storm there, we have to travel back all the way to 1858, when a Category 1 hurricane, simply known as the 1858 San Diego Hurricane, brushed the coast of San Diego County and brought tropical-storm-force winds to the region. San Diego of the 1850s had a fraction of the population it has today, but the storm still caused significant damage.

While weaker than the 1858 hurricane, the only tropical storm known to have made landfall on the California coast was a 1939 tropical storm that hit Long Beach, in Los Angeles County. It brought tropical-storm-force winds across a large swath of Southern California, along with over 4 inches of rain in some areas.

That storm was a surprise, and the United States Weather Bureau – the precursor to the modern National Weather Service – opened a Southern California office in 1940 in response. A 2004 research paper hypothesized that if a similar storm hit the region in the mid-2000s, it would have likely caused over US$200 million in damage to the region.

While a few other tropical storms in the 1970s came close to a landfall in California, all weakened or changed course, avoiding a direct hit. This includes the remnants of Hurricane Hilary in 2023 that were still strong enough to cause widespread flooding in Southern California and dump 10 inches of rain in the mountains.

A handful of additional systems that made landfall in Baja California or stayed offshore have brought tropical-storm-force winds to the state, including Hurricane Nora in 1997.

In addition, multiple recent storms over the open ocean have generated swells that damaged port and pier infrastructure in the region, including hurricanes Marie in 2024, Narda in 2025 and another Marie in 2026.

Several environmental factors increase the probability of tropical storms making an approach to Southern California.

The most notable is El Niño. This natural climate pattern, defined by unusually warm water in the eastern tropical Pacific, increases the frequency of storms in the eastern North Pacific. That’s because warmer than normal sea surface temperatures in the region are necessary to support the formation and development of these storms.

Even during El Niño years, the waters off the coast of Southern California and northern Baja California are typically too cool to support hurricanes. Still, storms moving fast enough or with enough support from upper-level winds can survive these slightly cooler temperatures, allowing the system to make an approach toward California.

When Tropical Storm Rachel began its approach toward Southern California on Oct. 9, the National Hurricane Center noted that the sea surface temperatures were anomalously warm off the coast of Baja California and played a role in its potential to remain a tropical cyclone as it approached the coast.

Like most eastern Pacific tropical storms and hurricanes, the primary effect on California from these systems is rainfall.

Most of Southern California is arid and rarely receives rainfall during summer and early fall. Early reports showed Rachel dumped upward of 6 inches of rain in parts of Southern California, including over 1 inch at San Diego International Airport in one weekend. That inch of rain in San Diego is double the typical October precipitation there.

While those amounts may seem minuscule compared to what typically comes with a tropical storm or hurricane landfall in places like Florida, they can cause flash flooding in the normally dry Southwest. The National Hurricane Center warned of flash flooding in California and other parts of the Southwest before Rachel’s landfall.

Unique cases like Rachel show that Mother Nature can always go against conventional wisdom, and, given enough time and the right conditions, potentially destructive things can happen.

Assistant Professor of Environmental Studies, University of Tampa

Billy Crystal doesn't trust God after Pacific Palisades fire and Rob Reiner's death

Billy Crystal opens up about the loss of his Pacific Palisades home and longtime friend Rob Reiner, ahead of the debut of his one-man Broadway show “860.”

Actual Article Body:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here.

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search.   Set us as preferred

Billy Crystal  no longer trusts God.

Following the 2025 loss of his home in the Pacific Palisades wildfires and the killing of his longtime collaborator, Rob Reiner, the 78-year-old actor has a newfound skepticism, he told “CBS Sunday Morning” correspondent Tracy Smith in an interview that aired last weekend.

Smith asked Crystal if he had been talking to God over these last couple of years, given that he recounted his conversations with God in his 2004 Tony Award-winning play “700 Sundays” and he is now promoting his one-man Broadway show, “860,” which premieres Oct. 21 at the Imperial Theatre in New York City.

“No, ‘cause I don’t trust him,” Crystal responded. “Too many bad things have happened. The Earth is in bad shape. This is a weird, scary time, so no. Not anymore.”

This drastic change of faith comes after Crystal and his wife Janice Crystal (née Goldfinger) lost their 1930s ranch house in the Palisades wildfire in January 2025. The couple, who have been married since 1970, purchased the stucco home in 1979 to raise their daughters Jenny, now 53, and Lindsay, 48.

Not much remained after the blazing devastation, save for some rocks with uplifting engraved words like “welcome,” “patience” and “dream” that the family laid around the garden decades prior, he shared with People in a cover story published online Wednesday.

“Lindsay found the ‘laughter’ rock,” Crystal said. “So the fact that that was the first thing [we found], we’ll be OK.”

Television

The Tony Award-winning 2004 stage show is captured for HBO ‘to document for my kids and my grandkids’ his early family history.

The Palisades fire inspired  “860,” which is titled after his home address and touches on themes of luck and fate.

“I started thinking about this in a way that I think was separating me from the pain of what was happening,” Crystal told the outlet. “It was healing me at the same time.”

He underscores that the story is not about the fire itself, rather a journey that highlights resilience, laughter and love and “facing things you never thought were possible,” he shared.

The New York born-and-bred comedian first opened up about personal pain in “700 Sundays,” his autobiographical one-man play that touched on the death of his father, who died of a heart attack when Crystal was 15.  The production won the Tony Award for special theatrical event.

Rob Reiner’s career began on television, and after leaving “All in the Family” he continued to perform, transforming tonally into a sort of gentle Jewish Buddha onscreen.

Reiner and Crystal met in 1976 on the set of the CBS sitcom “All in the Family” and became fast friends. Encouragement from his longtime confidante and collaborator helped the comedian write about the loss of his beloved home before Reiner’s tragic killing in December 2025 alongside his wife, Michele, in Brentwood.

The “Monsters, Inc.” voice actor called their chemistry “undefinable.”

“I knew it from the first time we met. I knew it from that first week: ‘This is going to be a forever thing, I just know it,’” Crystal told People. “We laughed. We talked about all kinds of things. We were always interested in what each other was doing and grateful that we both were getting chances to do something even as we went our separate ways in projects.”

California

A group of Rob Reiner’s closest friends released a statement remembering him as a ‘passionate, brave citizen’ who worked to make the world a better place.

The actor also shared that he was not the first choice when it came to the role of Harry in “When Harry Met Sally…,” but after considering other actors — among them Albert Brooks, Tom Hanks and Michael Keaton — Reiner approached Crystal as if it were a scene from the 1989 romantic comedy itself.

“One day the call came, and he was almost upset by saying, ‘I always knew it was you,’” Crystal said.

In preparing for the premiere of “860,” which runs until Jan. 3, Crystal recalled a brief moment where he forgot Reiner was gone.

“I ran upstairs to the dressing room, and my first thought was: ‘I got to call Rob and tell him,’” Crystal said. “I don’t know if I don’t want that to keep happening or I do want it to keep happening.”
